blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That could contribute to respiratory distress syndrome, a little bit of extra work of breathing later on.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So what, if any, measures were contemplated to address that potential?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: There was a collective decision to start all three babies on antibiotics for presumed infection and then I recall that all three babies were started on CPAP to help support their breathing.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Who was party to that collective decision?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: There were three registrars present, one for each baby.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It was [Dr B]'s week of neonatal cover so I think we will have, all four of us, discussed it together and then made a uniform decision.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: From your recollection, you've just described in detail [Baby P]'s condition, was there anything of concern with either of his siblings?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: For [Baby O] I can say probably not. For the third sibling, I don't recall.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So absent any negative indicator in relation to [Baby R], was this decision to put them on antibiotics purely precautionary?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Absolutely.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If we look down the page, please. Is this a summary of your impression?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes. The impression is presumed sepsis, respiratory distress syndrome, and then to start establishing feeds, but that's not a priority at this moment.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Then the plan was to start CPAP with a residual pressure of 5.5 centimetres of water. IV fluids at 60ml per kilogram per day, IV antibiotics, the vitamin K injection that's given to all newborn babies. Then a blood gas measurement to be followed by a chest X-ray.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Dealing with the impression, firstly, what was the basis upon which sepsis was presumed?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I don't recall. It must have been something to do with mother's health.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Respiratory distress syndrome. What gave you that impression?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So faster breathing or increased work of breathing, and I suspect that it wasn't [Baby P] that this decision was made upon, it was a collective decision for all three babies.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. So in that regard, how does your approach differ when dealing with the twins or triplets or even quads, I suppose, as opposed to dealing with a singleton baby?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: If there is suspected to be an illness in one of the babies of an infective cause, they've all shared a common maternal blood supply, so you would treat all three babies in the same way.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. You noted the desire to establish feeds but you told us a moment or two ago that that wasn't a priority. And then you took us to the plan which included CPAP and the provision of intravenous fluids.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What is the relationship between the management of a newborn's respiratory needs and its nutritional needs?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So the muscles used for breathing and feeding are the same. If you have increased work of breathing, you will not able to take an adequate volume of milk feeds and you would then destabilise the breathing and you wouldn't get adequate nutrition anyway.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So to which need do you give priority?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Breathing always first. And knowing that the breathing is taken care of by CPAP and with this baby being only -- well, certainly at this point less than an hour old, to give IV fluids whilst the breathing stabilises and whilst the work of breathing is observed to be normal, we wouldn't push a baby to take feeds orally if there were concerns about the breathing.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So going down our plan to point 3, and intravenous antibiotics, of course the triplets were born early and if I were to remind you that their mother had been given steroids prior to their birth, does that help inform or remind you as to the basis as to why they were prescribed antibiotics?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The steroids are given to help generate surfactant in the babies, to make their work of breathing easier when they are born, but it can also contribute to a slightly reduced response to infection in mum, so it would leave the babies more open to infection.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Are you able to assist as to the duration of the intended provision of antibiotics?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The blood cultures will have been taken at the time of putting the cannula in. Those results are usually available within 36 to 48 hours.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. We have what appear to be venous gas results; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Was there anything within those results to cause you any concern whatsoever?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: They are normal results for a recently born baby. The pH is normal. PCO2, the pressure of carbon dioxide, is up very slightly but this is a venous gas rather than a capillary gas that's normally taken, so this blood has already been through the peripheral circulation and is -- so I would accept a slightly higher carbon dioxide in that. Bicarbonate is normal. The base excess is only very slightly off normal; it's usually plus 2 to minus 2. The blood glucose is acceptable for a newborn baby and the lactate is very slightly elevated, but again this is a venous gas.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. So looking at those factors together, what was the quality of his gas results?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: These are acceptable. This is a perfectly satisfactory gas for starting CPAP. This baby doesn't need ventilating mechanically.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And does your final note on this page inform us that you did indeed place him on CPAP?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "To repeat in 90"; is that minutes?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It is.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that to repeat the blood gas test?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Can we return to the carousel, please. So that's mid-afternoon, 21 June 2016.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You had continuing involvement with [Baby P]; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Would you at every turn remind yourself of any relevant notes made by colleagues in between your direct involvement with the baby?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If we could just look briefly, please -- Mr Murphy, I'm not sure this is on the carousel, but if you could put up page J23840, please, which are notes written the following morning, ie 22 June, by your consultant colleague, [Dr B].
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Notes made at 11.45, 22 June. If you just appraise yourself of the contents there, [Dr A], without necessarily taking us
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: through the detail; [Dr B] will do so, I anticipate, in due course. But what's the quality of the baby's presentation as of the morning of the 22nd?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Overnight and into the following morning, [Baby P] has made no change. He's stable, he's on CPAP still. He's now in air, doesn't require any additional oxygen. His fluids are still being run through his peripheral cannula at the same rate and I think he is to be given a dose of caffeine in order to stimulate his respiratory drive. He's to have some blood tests later that day and a gas and this looks like progression. Nothing has happened that's a concern.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm grateful. Back to the carousel then, please, Mr Murphy. Let's go to 23 June and tile 64, which is a note made by your colleague Dr Cooke, who was, I think, at the time a locum senior house officer. Does that accord with your recollection?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Who had cause to examine [Baby P] in between your examinations of him at 10 am on 23 June. If we could just look at Dr Cooke's corresponding note in her distinctively neat handwriting. Have you previously reminded yourself of the contents of this clinical note?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I've not seen this note since the day in question, but I do recall the content of it.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If you care to refresh your memory from it before I ask you some general questions.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: (Pause). Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm grateful. "No nursing concerns" speaks for itself, as does indeed, I imagine, "Observations normal".
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Can you tell us what had happened with regards to the antibiotics that you and your colleagues prescribed to all three triplets?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It says:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Presumed sepsis. Antibiotics stopped on the 23rd."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the 36 hours of the blood culture incubation was completed, it's returned no positive results, and as [Baby P] is in good health with no new concerns, the antibiotics have been stopped.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Let's move to ventilation and respiration.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Self-ventilating in air, which means no additional support is required. Then feeding has progressed normally, as it does in those first few days of life, going from 60 to 75 to 90ml per kilogram per day, and this is now being administered by a nasogastric tube.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: There's a trace of aspirates and this is donor-expressed breast milk. [Baby P] has passed urine and opened his bowels.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: When we considered your note as of 21 June, for the reasons you explained to us (inaudible) respiration being given priority, he was to receive nutrition intravenously, but by now, is this right, on the morning of 23 June, he was being given expressed breast milk?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Any indication as to the output? Output all good, it would appear, by the "PU/BO [tick] [tick]"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What about jaundice? Was that a factor at all with [Baby P]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It's not been commented on, so normally if there is a concern about a colour change then a bilirubin would have been tested. It has been tested here and it's well below the treatment line. So this may well just have been added on to the normal biochemistry tests that are sent.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Would that just go with the territory (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Very much so, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- baby? Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If we could go down the page to see what it was that your colleague saw upon examination. Just taking those points of examination together, is there anything within that to sound any alarms whatsoever?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No. That's a completely normal newborn examination.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Amongst other features of the plan, including, as one would expect, the continuation of the establishment of feeds, there was to be a cranial ultrasound test; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What's the final entry at plan, point 4?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: "Vitamins and minerals prescribed."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Having commended Dr Cooke's handwriting --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It's clearly "prescribed" (overspeaking) and it looks as though it's "vita and mins".
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR A: Normally for preterm babies they would get folic acid on a Friday and multi-vitamins once they've established feeding and then, at day 28 of life, they'd be given an iron supplement.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We can see your handwriting at the bottom of the page; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: And does this correspond to plan point 3, cranial ultrasound?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It does.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is this your subsequent review of that ultrasound?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes. So between the end of Dr Cooke's entry and this entry, maybe even slightly before Dr Cooke had seen [Baby P], I will have done the cranial ultrasound, I will have looked at the images, and this was just the opportunity for [Dr B] to look at them and we've written in there that there were no concerns about any intracranial problems.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So you and [Dr B] have considered the ultrasound, discussed what it contained, and you are together jointly happy with the results?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: (Inaudible) "Normal appearance", is it?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR A: "Normal appearance. No evidence of haemorrhage or dilatation."
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Which we've seen, that phrase, before.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR A: Yes. There's no blood in any of the ventricles and the ventricles are all the right size. There's no abnormality.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Was this investigation made in consequence of any specific concern relating to [Baby P] or is this part of the protocols?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It's normal and usual for lower birth weight babies and preterm babies.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Go back to the carousel, please, Mr Murphy, and if we could remind ourselves of the greater chronology here and remind ourselves that, sadly, [Baby P]'s brother, [Baby O], died at 17.47 hours on 23 July 2016.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If we just look at notes made that morning. If we could move forward in time, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You told us earlier how the management, clinical management, of twins or triplets is often, to some extent, influenced by anything that might pertain to their brothers or sisters. Do you recall whether anything in particular was done or looked at in relation to [Baby P] as a consequence of [Baby O]'s early demise?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: There will have been a concern that there was an infective process going on and [Baby P] will have been re-examined and there would have been a very low threshold to start next line antibiotics.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Let's go to tile 134 then, please. Again to give time and the sequence context, [Baby O]'s death was at 17.47, and now at 18.00 hours, click behind, we'll see -- and if we go to the clinical notes, please -- that a colleague of yours, again it's Dr Cooke, of course it is, made a note of a review of [Baby P] undertaken principally by your consultant colleague, Dr Gibbs.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We'll hear in due course that this was done because of [Baby O]'s death.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could you summarise the results there for us, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: [Baby P] has a temperature of 36.6 degrees. He's selfventilating in air. His respiratory rate and heart rate are normal. He has been tolerating his nasogastric feeds. On examination he's active when handled, his perfusion is normal with a normal capillary refill time.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: He has no -- a normal respiratory pattern. His chest sounds clear, his abdomen is full, mildly distended, but no...
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Tenderness.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR A: No tenderness.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "No murmurs", is it?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR A: I wouldn't have thought so there:
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "No masses. Bowel sounds active. Mild erythema at the base of the umbilicus. No swelling or exudate. Femorals..."
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I would assume that that means femoral pulses, they were normal and his heart sounds were also normal.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Is "present", perhaps, after the word "femorals"?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Mild erythema at the base of the umbilicus."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could you expand on that for us?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The umbilicus is a potential source of infection and the infection, if it is at the umbilicus, has a direct route into the major blood vessels because that's where baby has been attached to the placenta until recently. The umbilicus starts to dry out over a few days and then drops off but in that time the circulation and the cord is drying out, it becomes a potential route in for infection. Any redness or signs of flaring, so like a little flame sign around the umbilicus, is a potential skin infection that may travel.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The plan of action at this point in time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So full blood count and CRP, looking for markers of infection or inflammation. A blood culture to see if any bacteria can be grown. Another bilirubin. Then to start cefotaxime a second-line antibiotic, and because of the erythema of the umbilicus, flucloxacillin has been started, which is used to treat cellulitis or skin infections. And the last point is abdominal X-ray because of the slight distension.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So these investigations and responses are in part because of [Baby O] and in part because of [Baby P]'s own presentation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that fair?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. At tile 289, please. We'll go to the second tile behind it rather than the original notes. It's a note made by your colleague, Dr Ukoh, who will give evidence himself today, which evidences, now that we have moved forward in time,
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Ukoh's examination of [Baby P] on the morning of Friday, 24 June, which records, amongst other things, that the:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Abdomen moderately distended/bloated. Soft."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And he was to be kept nil by mouth for now.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Ukoh will assist us in that regard in due course I'm sure. Let's move now to your next direct involvement, please, which I think is at tile 295. So if we go to the original clinical note, please, Mr Murphy. Before we look at the detail, can you remember the nature of your duties on that day, that is to say Friday, 24 June?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes. I was the long day registrar, so I would have typically started working on the children's ward rather than the neonatal unit. I would have been responsible for the ward round on the children's ward and then overseeing any admissions that came through the admissions area.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We can see from this long note, which you have timed at intervals, that as per the note at 09.40, you were called to the neonatal intensive care unit; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Does the note suggest that, having been so called, you arrived at about 09.50?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Thereabouts, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What was the reason given to you that invited you to attend immediately?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I don't remember the phone call itself. I remember being bleeped and then by answering that bleep I will have been asked to come. It wasn't a crash bleep, so I finished doing or putting away the notes that I was dealing with at the time and then I made my way to the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So not communicated to you as an emergency?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I think it was, "Can you come quickly?" but it wasn't, "Drop everything and run". I was there fairly quickly.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And please help us understand what it is that you saw and ascertained at about 09.50 or thereabouts?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: [Baby P] was in nursery 2. He had the incubator space on the right-hand side and I think it was the furthest from the door, closest to the window. When I got there he had a heart
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: rate that was approximately 80 beats a minute and his oxygen saturations were approximately 60%.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: He was being bagged by a Neopuff circuit and the pressures on the wall that was delivered through that circuit had an inspiratory pressure of 20 centimetres of water and a PEEP of 5. At that time he was being bagged in air.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Pausing there one moment, please, if you would help us understand. The heart rate at 80 is plainly lower than previous readings. How low a heart rate and how great a cause for concern is a rate of 80?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: 80 is lower than I would expect of a baby of [Baby P]'s gestation and now age. It is likely that the heart rate has dropped because the oxygen saturations have dropped; one precedes the other.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: How significant a drop in oxygen saturation level?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's too low. Normally, I would be expecting the saturation to be above 92%.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: He was being bagged already upon your arrival; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Were you content with that response and did you deem the levels of ventilation provided appropriate to the prevailing conditions?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I will have been given some information, and I don't recall what information or by who. And as with other babies, I will have gone to the head end of the incubator and taken over management of the airway. At this time his oxygen saturations were improved by using a device that lifts the tongue out of the way and makes the airway more patent.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that the --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It's a Guedel airway.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Was that part of your management of the airway, as you --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I think it will have been me, but it will have been a very busy nursery at that time with people aiming to assist as much as they can.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the use of the Guedel seemed to improve the effects of the already ongoing Neopuffing?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It's an adjunct. It's used for stabilisation but you wouldn't maintain a baby with a Guedel airway. So this is telling me that this baby needs to be intubated.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Hence you did so at the first attempt?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The size of the tube?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: A 3.0-millimetre diameter tube and it's secured at 8 centimetres at the lips.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You have told us previously that you were at this point an experienced intubator. Were you satisfied as to the appropriateness of the size of the intubation tube as per a baby of this size, weight and gestation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It was the tube that I would have calculated based on his age and his weight. I recall that it was an easy tube to site and it was very easy to get it in and I was relieved to see that there was a good colour change on the capnograph indicator. I seem to remember that later on in the day I've replaced it with a 3.5 diameter tube.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. So as of your arrival and attendance upon [Baby P], you have just explained to us how you took control of the management of the airway and how it would appear, from the indicators available to you, that it had been a success.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Was that management of the airway the immediate priority?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, it was.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We can see a list of blood gas results down the left margin of the page, which may or may not also correspond to 09.51 or may just happen to be there on your note.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: But were these blood gas results taken at around this time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I think these will be the exact times that were on the paper slips that were printed from the blood gas machine.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you for that. What was the nature and/or quality of those results?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The gas at 09.51 is a poor gas. 7.15 as a pH is lower than the 7.25-plus that I would desire. Carbon dioxide is elevated. The bicarbonate is normal. The base excess is much larger than I would expect. Blood glucose is normal. The lactate is much higher than I would have expected.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Considered individually and/or taken together, what did these results inform you of?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So this is a metabolic gas. This is a metabolic acidosis with also some components of a respiratory acidosis.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Did those results inform you of anything additional to that which you had observed by his condition and his respiratory struggles upon your arrival?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: This is a gas that suggests over the previous 15 to 30 minutes, [Baby P] has been working hard, in part with his respiration, but actually there's a lot of metabolic information there.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Did that steer your immediate course?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It will have directed me to make sure that the airway is secure and stable and I would imagine that given that lactate, a fluid bolus will have been considered.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And accordingly, what did you do? If we continue to look down the page.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: [Baby P]'s been started on continuous mandatory ventilation; the pressures are there on the right-hand side. They are normal settings for a baby of his age and size.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: He is in 75% oxygen with a mandatory rate of 60 breaths a minute. At 10.15 he's been given some bicarbonate and that will be because the subsequent gas at 10.06 has a lower bicarbonate value than the one at 09.51. And the lactate is increasing.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Let's take that chronologically then. You have managed the airway in the way you've described and then, some 15 minutes or so later, there was a subsequent set of blood gas results. Did they indicate satisfactory improvement or did they give you further cause for concern?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No, [Baby P]'s continuing to deteriorate. The carbon dioxide level has increased. The base excess has increased and the lactate has increased. Subsequently his glucose has also increased but that's likely a stress response to the other components that are there.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So notwithstanding what you deemed to be satisfactory management of the airway, he went backwards rather than forwards?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And in consequence, what, if anything, did you do?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So at 10.15 -- no, sorry, adrenaline was given at 9.55, 10.02, 10.08, 10.15 and 11.10. But the doses there will be given because of the poor heart rate, poor perfusion, and that will have led to a secondary sort of poor respiratory drive, which is why he's on continuous mandatory ventilation.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You have just explained to us the reason why adrenaline was deemed to be required. Can you remind us as to the purpose of the use of bicarbonate in this context?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Bicarbonate is used in metabolic acidosis and it's either given as a half correction or a full correction dose and that's based on the pH and the bicarbonate level on the gas.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We can see is it at 10.15, and possibly additionally at 11.10, there's what you termed a loading dose of morphine; is that right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What's the purpose of that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Morphine is used to sedate babies who are being ventilated.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Just for comfort?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It's so that they can tolerate the tube. Without that degree of sedation, and there's a little bit of analgesia that goes with it, it may be uncomfortable to have that tube there and baby may well then fight that ventilator.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So pain relief and comfort and making more compliant?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Before we leave this part of your note we can see a list of digits to the right of the page, is that the level of ventilation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes. The inspiratory pressure, the peak inspiratory patient, the peak end expiratory pressure, the fraction of time,
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: TI, on inspiration. The ventilator setting for oxygen is 75% and the mandatory respiratory rate is 60 breaths per minute.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. We can see another entry just before you time the next set of events at 11.30. Your final entry prior to that is timed at 10.46. What was the impression, what was the position in relation to [Baby P]'s apparent direction of travel as of 10.46?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So this is an improvement. His pH has improved and I think that may say 7.829, in which case his pH has become slightly too alkaline. His carbon dioxide level has is reduced because of the ventilation. His base excess has improved compared to the previous gas and his lactate there, I think, is 10.5, which is a slight improvement on the previous gas from 25 minutes ago.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: His gases were improving a little. Do you recollect how [Baby P] appeared to you at this point, 10.46?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I don't have a picture of him in my head. I do remember that the room was incredibly busy. There will have been lots of equipment around for intubation and making sure that his venous access was adequate. There will have been a lot of attention being paid to the bedside monitors and there will have been quite regular checks on breathing, heart rate, blood pressure.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: At the very least the blood gas results, as considered at 10.46, tend to indicate something of an improving position?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The lactate reading --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR A: Yes?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: -- what do you think it is?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR A: I think that that is either 10.5 or 13.5. I can't tell whether the margin line...
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Perhaps Mr Murphy can zoom in.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That does look like 13.5.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: How does that compare?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR A: That's slightly worse than the previous gas at 10.06.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Lactate is going to be a slow marker to improve because the components of the gas that demonstrate a metabolic acidosis need to be corrected first and then the lactate will stop being
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: produced. A lot of this will then be down to perfusion and the amount of sort of circulatory output that [Baby P] has.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Whilst we've got the note blown up, could you return your attention to the pH, please?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It does look like 7.829.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Mr Myers is helpfully showing me the same data on a different document, which tends to suggest that that measurement there is 7.229.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: In which case that's -- compared to the previous gas this is markedly improved and I would be quite happy that the respiratory component is much better, the pH has started to normalise. It will take some time for the lactate to follow the direction that the bicarbonate has taken after the bicarbonate has been administered.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So taking a step back, based on the blood gas results in any event, how did things appear to be moving as of 10.46?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: This indicates that over the last 20 to 25 minutes, the blood gas measurements are improving.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Forgive me, please, I'm just looking at the measurement report, which confirms that which Mr Myers helpfully pointed out to us, that the pH reading at this point is 7.229.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It looks like a 2 has been overscored on to another number underneath the 2.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR A: It does.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: And that's consistent with the other thing, so Mr Myers is right in his assertion it's 7.229.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: [Dr A], the jury will have this in due course but don't have it just yet. In that file in front of you, that's the very one, behind divider 21, there is a bundle of documents towards the back of which, five from the back, is the measurement report, which in the bottom right-hand corner should have, in red ink, stamped J23961.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that the report from which your note is derived?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So for the avoidance of all doubt, if any still remains, the pH level?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And the lactate level?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So now that you have that report in front of you, do you wish to, in any way, revise or refine your evidence as to his general position and the direction of travel as of 10.46?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: As of 10.46 this is no longer a respiratory acidosis.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The ventilation has taken care of the carbon dioxide.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The component of this gas that is making him acidotic is metabolic and that is based on the bicarbonate readings, which are now lower, and a lactate which suggests that those cells are struggling to metabolise normally.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm grateful. Let's move on in time to the next episode, as it were, and if we leave this screen on in this way, we can read it clearly. There are half a dozen or so clinical -- lines of clinical note timed at 11.30. Just remind yourself of what it is you noted and then describe to the jury what occurred from 11.30 onwards.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: At 11.30 there was an episode of desaturation and bradycardia. In response to that, cardiopulmonary resuscitation was recommenced.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Pausing there, you used the word recommenced. We saw immediately above the introduction of adrenaline and the like in response to his poor condition. Was there as part of that, that earlier episode, that from about 09.51 onwards, was there cardiopulmonary resuscitation involved in that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I don't recall that, but certainly having said recommenced it would suggest that there had been even a brief period of CPR.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: In any event, CPR certainly was involved at 11.30 onwards?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Can you describe that episode to the jury, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So [Baby P]'s heart rate will have been less than 60 beats per minute and that in the context of a lower oxygen level, he will have either been bagged through the tube using a Neopuff circuit or -- no, he will have been bagged through the Neopuff because the tube was removed at that time. He was given adrenaline at 11.32 and then pancuronium -- sorry, 11.32, with the adrenaline at 11.30.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Pancuronium is a profound relaxant; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Was that given to, again, make the baby compliant with the ventilatory intervention?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes. So pancuronium will have been given because [Baby P] will have appeared to have been fighting the ventilator.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: He will have been putting in breaths against it or not taking breaths alongside the ventilation. Pancuronium was given because it takes a few minutes to become active but it lasts for about an hour and a half.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We can see from your notes that the duration of this episode was relatively brief, that is to say from 11.30 to 11.36 approximately.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Obviously. And how did it go?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So the medications and the CPR have been successful and at 11.36, [Baby P] has restored his own spontaneous circulation and I would imagine he has re-synchronised with the ventilator.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That ventilation, as previously applied, was that recommenced thereafter?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes. I would expect given that as the previous gas had shown good ventilatory response, he will have been recommenced on the same settings.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If we continue down the page, please. At 12.08, was there a further set of blood gas results considered?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes. This is 30 minutes since the end of CPR and he had been restored to continuous mandatory ventilation. At this point the pH is very good, it's sort of within normal limits if not slightly too much. And the carbon dioxide level is a little lower than I would wish. His bicarbonate is remaining roughly in the same place. And his base excess again is a little bit worse
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: than the previous gas. In response to the carbon dioxide being a little bit low I've reduced the inspiratory pressure on the ventilator from 23 down to 20. That gives a little less inflation pressure and so it stops him blowing off as much carbon dioxide, so I'm going to allow him to retain a little bit more.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So some fine-tuning of the ventilatory assistance?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Moving to your next note, timed at 12.28, and the final note on this page.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: "12.28. Desaturation and bradycardia again. CPR commenced."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: As part of this, the capnograph has been reattached to the endotracheal tube and there's poor colour change on it. The tube was removed and [Baby P] was bagged just using the Neopuff circuit placed over his mouth and nose.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We'll come to the remainder of your note in a moment and we've been here in your evidence previously, but please remind us what significance you would have attached to the poor colour change on the ET capnograph at this juncture in all these circumstances.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: In the time since... Poor colour change suggests there's not very much carbon dioxide passing up through the ET tube. You'd normally expect the capnograph to blanche and flush with each breath and that's not happening. The first bit of kit that gets looked at is the tube itself as it might be coated by secretions, it may be blocked by mucus. So the tube has been removed and then conventional bagging has been done with the Neopuff circuit.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: My Lord, we're about to move on to another period of CPR and the like and there are more episodes to deal with. Is this a convenient point, please?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, certainly.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: [Dr A], we'll break off there and resume again at 2 o'clock.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: 2 o'clock, please, members of the jury.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The short adjournment)
Could I invite Mr Stansfield's assistance to distribute the paper bundles in relation to [Baby P]?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: There's one for his Lordship there and 12 for the jury.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: There's one already in the witness box folder, as we know.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: (Handed)
These will go behind divider 21 in due course but perhaps you might benefit from just keeping them at hand for the moment whilst we refer to them from time to time.

[Dr A], we were just looking on screen at your notes corresponding to results obtained and/or considered at 12.08, which include a base excess reading, according to your notes at least, of minus 13.4; do you see that?
DR A: Yes, I do.

I don't think we have the corresponding printout for this particular set of results. If you look at the paper bundle in front of you and go to the third document, to the back, which is a blood gas record chart on which various sets of results have been recorded for [Baby P]. Do you have that? It's stamped J23979 in the bottom right corner.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, I do.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. If we look at the corresponding entry for 12.08, that is to say the penultimate entry on this document, we can see it largely corresponds to the data that you recorded on the clinical notes that we have on screen. I say largely because there is a discrepancy between the base excess as recorded in your note as compared to that recorded on the blood gas record document within the bundle, yours being a note of minus 13.4 and the author of this document recording the same entry at minus 11.4.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Other than that, they appear to correspond, the sets of data. As a matter of interest, which reading is more concerning, a base excess of minus 13.4 or one of minus 11.4?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Minus 13.4 is more concerning, but anything above minus 2, or greater than minus 2, is abnormal.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. So having just alluded to that apparent discrepancy and observing, as I have already, that as far as I am aware the original document is not available, you continued to take us through the narrative of events and we had got as far as the tube -- removal of the tube at or around 12.28 because that was a potential cause or contributor to the problem.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And [Baby P] was bagged via Neopuff. I think we have to jump to tile 420 to see the remainder of your clinical note.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Click on the original document, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do you recognise this as a continuation of the note that we left --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- immediately before lunch? So did you re-intubate the baby?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You already anticipated this earlier in your evidence by noting the difference in size between the first tube and the second.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: This one is the next size of tube up and I will have noted when I put the 3.0 in that it was a good fit.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: This will have been more of a snug fit.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Was the event of re-intubation at 12.32?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And what did you do immediately thereafter?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Following that, I was happy that the airway was secure and, by the notes here, [Baby P]'s heart rate was still not improving, so he's been given adrenaline through a peripheral cannula and then a number of adrenaline boluses given through that cannula at the corresponding times.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Just for one second returning to the original ET tube, you've explained to us the reasons or some of the reasons why you withdrew it. Do you recall whether or not, as a matter of fact, you checked it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I don't recall checking it.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's return to this episode then. Your notes suggested all episodes of desaturation and bradycardia were accompanied by -- could you read the rest of the note for us, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: "... profound colour change and poor central and peripheral perfusion."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What, if anything, was that profound colour change and poor central and peripheral perfusion --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It suggests what his heartbeat and his cardiac output were insufficient to maintain normal colour, either within the central circulation and more extreme at the peripheral, both fingers and toes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We saw earlier a reference to the desire to consider -take and consider a chest X-ray.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Was that done at this point?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That looks as though it happened at around about 12.30 and it showed a right-sided lateral pneumothorax, so there will be a partial collapse of the lung on the right-hand side and this was decompressed by putting a small cannula into that space to relieve the air and allow the lung to re-inflate.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So that problem, as identified on the chest X-ray at 12.30, was immediately upon consideration addressed?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The X-ray machines have a small screen on them and because he was acutely unwell at the time, we will have looked at the Xray on the screen rather than wait for it to be uploaded to the system and look at it on a PC.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's continue down your note if we may.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What was the next course of action?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: At 12.51 another bicarbonate was administered. That will have been in response to a low bicarbonate or a metabolic component to his later gas.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: At 12.55 another bolus of 10ml per kilogram of normal saline. Then because of concerns about blood pressure and cardiac output, dobutamine was started at 13.10 at a rate of 20 micrograms per kilogram.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Fifteen minutes later, at 13.25, another bicarbonate dose was given and that was after [Dr B] had had a telephone conversation with Dr Rackham -- I'm not sure whether Dr Rackham was on site at that time or whether he was travelling.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Rackham, we know, is the transport consultant.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: He was.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Was there any improvement in [Baby P]'s circulation, firstly, post the decompression of the right-sided pneumothorax?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The decompression of the pneumothorax with a cannula is a very temporary measure. It will have allowed the air to be released, it will have allowed the lung to re-inflate and fill the gap that was occupied by air previously. That will need addressing in a little bit.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The infusions that were started will have had some effect initially but it will be more in watching what happens to the trend of his blood pressure and heart rate and then also by looking at how he appears visually.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: How was he doing during this period between 12.50 and 13.25?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: My only memory of this bit is that it was very, very busy, both in looking at [Baby P] and seeing how he was progressing -and I think at that point I will have been setting up ready to put a chest drain in as a definitive treatment for his pneumothorax.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Was that something that had already been discussed with Dr Rackham?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It may well have been. Leaving that cannula in to decompress the pneumothorax is, as I said, only a temporary measure, it will need something more durable.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's continue down the note then, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So at 14.30 metronidazole and hydrocortisone were both given. Hydrocortisone will have been because of concerns about cardiac output and blood pressure.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Metronidazole was a further treatment for any presumed infection as this was potentially still an episode that we were looking at caused by sepsis. And at that time also, the ventilator will have been detached from [Baby P]'s ET tube and a dose of surfactant, this 240 milligrams of Curosurf, will have been
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: given down the ET tube directly into the lungs, hence the batch number there beneath.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Up until this point to what degree did breathing seem to be a fundamental component of his problems?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It was a major component. The work of breathing and the effect that that inefficient breathing was having on the blood gases and then subsequently, presumably, driving a metabolic component, there was no clearly identifiable cause as to what was going on. We were managing symptoms as they arose.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the dominant symptoms were, to recap?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Difficulty in breathing, low cardiac output, low blood pressure.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Were you able to identify any apparent cause for any one of those dominant symptoms?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Let's continue down the page, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: At 15.00 -- you told us already, I believe, that pigtail chest drains were inserted. How did that go?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The procedure itself was very straightforward. Setting up for it and securing the chest drain was a work of only a couple of minutes. The landmarks of putting that chest drain in were easily identifiable.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What was of the objective behind that intervention?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That was so that if any further -- the pneumothorax means that there's some air leaking from lung into the chest cavity, it wasn't being contained within the lung completely. So the chest drain is there to allow any air that escapes to be directly let out to the outside world so that the lung can be completely inflated with air through the ventilator.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You told us that there was no apparent cause for any of the dominant problems, yet you've also alluded to the existence of a pneumothorax.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Was that considered as a cause?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It's a potential cause. It will certainly have been playing a part in the respiratory part of the blood gases. When
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: that pneumothorax occurred is unclear and with a small pneumothorax, as this one appeared on that initial chest X-ray, I didn't want it to become any bigger, hence the drain being inserted, but I don't think this was the sole driver of all of the symptoms.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: May it have been a consequence of the symptoms --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Potentially --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- and your response to it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes. The ventilation that [Baby P] had been receiving were not at very high pressures, they were at pressures at the upper end of normal. It is possible that in the part of the morning where [Baby P] had been fighting the ventilator, the pneumothorax may have occurred then.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Let's continue down the page, please. So we can see, as to the introduction of the pigtail drains, the lung re-expanded, did it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So that was successful?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And this was reviewed or discussed with both Drs Rackham and [Dr B]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: At 13.38 we have what appear to be further blood gas results; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Anything of significance as a result or the pattern of results?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The pH is acceptable. The bicarbonate -- sorry, the carbon dioxide is on the lower end of normal, if not slightly low. The bicarbonate continues to remain low.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The base excess is elevated. Then we have a blood glucose that is much higher than previous readings and that lactate continues to be running high.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Based on this gas, with that CO2 being a little bit on the low side, the mandatory rate on the ventilator was reduced from 60
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: breaths per minute down to 50 breaths per minute to allow a little bit more carbon dioxide to be retained.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If we continue to look at your contribution to the clinical notes, we will need to go to our tile 545 to do so. If we could click on to the original note, please, timed at 15.14.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Did [Baby P] at about this point in time go into a cardiac arrest?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, he did. At 15.14, CPR was commenced. Adrenaline was given at 15.15 and then 15.20. A dose of sodium bicarbonate -this is, I think, a full correction rather than a half correction -- was given at 15.17.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: His oxygen saturations remain between 50% to 60% in 100% oxygen given through the ventilator. Heart rate remained low. Chest compressions were maintained and they were continuous.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We know from your evidence about earlier events that the threshold of 60 or below for a heart rate is an automatic trigger to this sort of intervention or response; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And equally, his saturations levels, as recorded here, is another indicator of grave concern?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So did the response protocol kick in and did you observe all established steps?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes. In the outline below, another dose of adrenaline at 15.24, bicarbonate at 15.29. Another adrenaline at 15.30 and 15.35, and a further note at 15.40.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It described as "high dose" there. Should we attach any significance to the adjective "high" in this context?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I forget what the actual calculated dose would have been but the fact that I have recorded it as high would suggest that, through either discussion with [Dr B] or Dr Rackham, we had decided that -- that was the dose that was decided on to try and generate a response.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Now the screen has scrolled down, we can see the continuation of the attempted use of adrenaline as part of the response. We can see that at 15.49, you record the introduction of atropine. What is the desired objective of that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Atropine is another resuscitation drug. It's there to support cardiac output.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Further adrenaline at 15.54. Then you make a note about the waveform monitor; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Can you interpret that for the jury, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Throughout the morning [Baby P] will have had chest leads attached at locations across the chest to pick up cardiac output and that's displayed on the monitoring screen above the incubator. At this time, at 15.54, there will have been the appearance of a waveform on the screen that's not corresponding to any discernible pulse or heartbeat and it's given the term pulseless electrical activity. There's electrical activity that can be seen on the screen, but it doesn't generate a response in the heart tissue to generate a pulse.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. In short, whatever the screen was indicating, there was no spontaneous heartbeat?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No, none.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What about his circulation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: There was no spontaneous circulation, either pulses in the femoral -- the pulses where you check just inside the nappy. blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, I was.

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And yet notwithstanding all of those efforts, there was sadly no cardiac output --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- or consequential circulation? Dr Rackham made a visual examination of [Baby P] and did all those factors combine to drive you, the clinicians, to the sad realisation that resuscitation was futile from hereon in?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The resuscitation had been at around about 45 minutes at this point, with no cardiac output. [Baby P]'s pupils didn't respond to light, they were fixed and dilated, and at that point the senior clinicians halted resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It was discussed with [Baby P]'s family.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Was that timed at 16.00 hours?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: [Dr A], you were involved directly in the care of [Baby P] from his birth, tragically, to his death.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Were you able to understand the course his life took over those few days?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Would you remain there, [Dr A], and answer any questions asked of you?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

Examination-in-chief by MR ASTBURY
