blocks.text: Yes. My name is Dr Anthony Ukoh.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Dr Ukoh, we've heard from you before. You've been invited along today to assist with your recollections of a shift on 24 June 2016 at the neonatal unit of the Countess of Chester Hospital and, in particular, your treatment of a little boy called [Baby P].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: In preparing your statement for today, have you had an opportunity to review your notes?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I've had a look at my notes and also of the actual statement that I made, yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Good. May I ask you whether you have any independent recollection of [Baby O] on 24 June 2016?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's mainly with the help of my notes being how long the incident has been.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Would it assist if we put the notes on the screen in front of you?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that'd be helpful, yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Could we go to tile 289, please, Mr Murphy?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We'll need to scroll down a little bit. Hopefully there we can see an entry at 9.35. Do you recognise the handwriting?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that is my handwriting.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Good. You've headed it "RWR"; is that "routine ward round"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, that is registrar ward round.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Apologies. You've timed it and dated it helpfully, and I think at the start of the note you've set out what you
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: understood to be the issues that [Baby P] had faced during the course of his short life.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That is correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Thank you. We'll go through those, please. You have noted his gestation at birth and his present age.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that, "(1) prematurity"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's a short form of prematurity.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: At number 2, you've recorded he was triplet number 1; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: What's the entry in brackets, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That is MCTA, which is a short form for monochorionic triamniotic.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's the type of triplets that the pregnancy was.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Is where the three triplets share the same placenta?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That is absolutely correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Number 3, RDS, we've heard about, is respiratory distress syndrome; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: And also you've noted that he had previously been on CPAP?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: You have noted at number 4 the occurrence of apnoeas and bradys, so bradycardias?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, correct.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: And you've also noted abdominal distension, number 5?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Nothing in number 6?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: That summarises your position as you understood it to be; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's very correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Again, this is a process we're becoming familiar with.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: V is ventilation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: So correct me if I'm wrong, is that self-ventilating in air?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That is correct.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: But notwithstanding that, there had been some desats and bradys?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: In your point 3, "Previous CPAP", does that suggest that [Baby P]'s no longer on CPAP and is (overspeaking) breathing for himself?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That is exactly what I meant, yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Feeding, is that F, nil by mouth?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Then you've noted the rate at which he is receiving 10% dextrose. Then is that bowels open and passed urine, both ticked?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Thank you. We can go to the next page, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You then list the medications which [Baby P] was receiving. Is that first one crossed out?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, because that was what he was on before. He wasn't on that now when I had come to see him, so that is crossed out, yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: You then put "re-screened", is that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: And a number 3?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Re screened on day 3."
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: And then you've listed cefotaxime, which we know is an antibiotic?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: And is that "fluclox" an abbreviation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's the short form of flucloxacillin, which is also an antibiotic.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: You've then examined [Baby P]; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: You have noted he was mildly pale?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Is that "zero recession"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that just means -- sorry, it's one of our shorthands for "no recession".
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Okay. Very briefly, please, recession being?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Recession is difficulty in breathing, so recession is what you normally see when you look at the anterior chest wall, the front of the chest. So there was no recession at that point.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: So despite being in air, no apparent difficulty --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: In breathing.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Thank you. I think that covers heart sounds, the next entry:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "1 plus 2 plus [is that] very soft systolic"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, on listening to the heart, there was a very soft murmur, which is sometimes what we hear with the stethoscope, but it was very soft, so it may have been nothing. Sometimes you could hear that and sometimes it just disappears as well.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Any cause for concern at that stage?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not with a very soft systolic murmur given he was only 3 days old. Nothing untoward.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Underneath that, is that "LSE"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, in is in reference to the systolic murmur and the LSE means at the left sternal edge. This is where the murmur was heard. So it wasn't everywhere, it was heard at a specific part of the chest wall, which again is showing that it's a probable innocent murmur, nothing really to worry about at that point.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Does the word "moderately" also refer to that feature?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, that refers to the distension of the abdomen.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Which is the next -- the abd. So there was moderate distension and some bloatedness. However, the abdomen was soft, so it wasn't hard at that point.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Would you have examined the abdomen as a consequence of what you saw?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Oh yes. This is the reference down below, that it was soft, so that's the examination of the abdomen.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Is that what you would hope to find in those circumstances?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You mean the distension?
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: The fact it was soft.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, it could be soft, it could be hard as well, but it wasn't normal to find a moderately distended abdomen that is bloated. But it was soft, so sometimes you can have it quite hard as well and it's a bit more worrying.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: You noted that the capillary refill time was less than 2 seconds.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, which is normal.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: And the skin, to you, was slightly mottled?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Thank you. Scroll up a little more, Mr Murphy, and we'll look at the plan, please, Dr Ukoh.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Number 1, is that "repeat bloods"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, repeat bloods.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Just take us through those abbreviations, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That FBC is a full blood count, which is one of the routine tests to check for anaemia. The second one is U&Es, which is urea and electrolytes, again fairly common if you are on a drip. The CRP is the C-reactive protein, which is a marker of infection. And the next one is a gas which just tells you about the breathing, the oxygen levels and other gases. Then you have the lactate, which is what you can use to measure perfusion, being that the skin was slightly mottled. And then an ammonia as well.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: What's the ammonia?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The ammonia is one of the tests that can be performed.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: If you're thinking of a metabolic condition, it's one of those non-specific tests that you could do. And if it's raised, it could point towards something metabolic.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Right. Number 2, is that:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Trial for long line for TPN"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: We've heard TPN is a means of feeding the baby when they're nil by mouth.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Absolutely, yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Then is number 3:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Keep nil by mouth for now"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: For now, yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Then I think we can see your signature thereafter.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Do you recall your overall impression of [Baby P] during your examination?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. My overall impression is this is a child we need to keep an eye on. However, at that point he wasn't particularly unwell. Being that he's premature and he had that distension, we
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: had to keep an eye on him, in particular in relation to a condition called NEC, necrotising enterocolitis.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: So that was the concern going forward?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And also infection as well, yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Okay. Anything else of note during the course of your examination before you left [Baby P] that morning?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I wouldn't say -- apart from that, you know, there wasn't anything else that I can remember, no.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Did you see him again shortly afterwards?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I saw him again but that was in a different context.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Tell us about that, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I cannot remember the exact -- where I was exactly, but it then became -- I would say maybe 20 minutes after I was called back to an alert that he was -- he had become quite unwell. So there was a sudden deterioration, he was nowhere like what he was after I'd seen him. So his oxygen levels had plummeted, his heart rate had also plummeted as well.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Okay. Just breaking that down, you think it was about 20 minutes later, did you say?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think. This is just in relation to -- looking at the notes, putting that all together, because I can only say that was the case because I was examining his brother.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: So I did put a note that I had to be called away from -- and it was around that time, it was at least 20 minutes that I made that time, yes. So roughly about that, yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: So his brother was [Baby R]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: His brother was [Baby R], yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: You were saying you were with [Baby R] when you were called away?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Absolutely, yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: You think about 20 minutes later. Do you remember where you were?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Still on the same unit, I think, yes. Still on the same unit.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: And do you recall who called you or how you came to go back to [Baby P]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: To be honest, I can't really remember. I can't really remember because it's been quite a while. I don't want to guess, yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: You started to tell us how different [Baby P] presented when you'd gone back after those 20 minutes or so. Just describe that to us, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. When I was -- when I saw -- you asked about [Baby P]?
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Yes, [Baby P], please. You told us you were called back to [Baby P] and I think you mentioned that he presented very differently than he had been presenting 20 minutes or so before. Just explain to us how he looked when you went back, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: When I'd seen [Baby P] about 20 minutes earlier he had a normal heart rate, his oxygen levels were fine, but on coming back -- when I was called back, his oxygen levels were, if I remember correctly, they were like 60% in air and his heart rate was 80 beats per minute, which is definitely not what it was when I was with him.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: I don't think you made another note, but did you, during the course of preparing your statement, have a look at [Dr B]'s note?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: We'll go to that in a minute then. Don't feel pressured to try and remember too much. Just from your own recollection, you told us that he wasn't well when you went back. Do you remember who else was there when you went back, if anybody?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I remember definitely [Dr B] being there. I think she was also doing the ward round with me if I can remember, just -- and with the notes that I had, yes. I know there were some nurses in there but I can't remember who exactly they were.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: All right. We've heard earlier from [Dr A]. Do you recall whether [Dr A] was there at that point?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Absolutely. Sorry, yes, he was there, yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Do you have any recollection of how [Dr A] came to be there?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: [Dr A] was called by a nurse, one of the nurses who was also there. I just can't remember who it was.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Do you remember anything, if you can't remember the name, anything about what the nurse was doing who had called [Dr A]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Again, this is just going by the notes, that is giving some kind of support with the bagging, so giving some face mask ventilation, which I also took over.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Was that request for [Dr A] after both you and [Dr B] were present?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: So it was a request for a third doctor to attend?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Was it a request by name or was it just for any other doctor?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, that was for [Dr A] in particular.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: You can't recall the name of the nurse who --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, no, I can't recall.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: You think it was whoever was doing the Neopuff at that particular moment?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. If I must say, why the nurse definitely wanted [Dr A] is that the day before [Dr A] had been involved with the sib, was heavily involved, that's the only reason why I could think we needed extra hands, that's the only reason why I could think the nurse wanted [Dr A] because there was a sib who unfortunately had a similar --
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: By sib, do you mean sibling?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. He was heavily involved with that one, so that's the only reason --
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Did the nurse say that was the reason why they wanted [Dr A]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I just assumed. I just assumed, yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Do you recall what you did when you went back to [Baby P]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Oh yes. Being that he had very low oxygen levels, his heart rate was low, I proceeded to give some face mask ventilations with the Neopuff. This is just giving some ventilation through a mask to support the breathing.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Without going to [Dr B]'s note, which I promised you we would, do you remember anything else about what happened during the course of that initial event?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So when [Dr A] came over, he wanted to take over the airway so we let him do that. So he took over the airways, he then proceeded to intubate the baby -- so that's putting down a breathing tube. Unfortunately, the access, the access that the baby had, which is a cannula --
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: This is intravenous access?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that got lost. So in that sort of situation to give very important medication we needed to have some access. So because of how urgent it was, we proceeded on to find intraosseous access. So I sited one and [Dr B] sited on the other leg as well.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: When you described access as lost, just explain that to us, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry. There was a previous cannula which was through the vein, so this is what I mean, that it actually -- it wasn't working anymore --
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Okay. Were you aware why?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sometimes it happens, sometimes babies just lose their cannulas and you have to re-site it. I don't know particularly why that happened then, but you know that's what happened, and it was very important that we re-site it to give fluids and other important medication.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: As it happens, we've heard a little bit about -- is it intraosseous access?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: So you sited one of those accesses; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. It was being done simultaneously, if I can remember. So I sited one and [Dr B] sited the other on each leg.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Okay. The purpose being to enable --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, to give drugs, fluids, yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Did you remain at the resuscitation to treat [Baby P] after that access had been secured?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: After that, because there was already [Dr B], [Dr A], and because there was two babies that had to be seen on that morning ward round, I then proceeded on to carry on with the round.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: I did say we'd look at that note, I think you've probably covered it, but can we look at tile 625, Mr Murphy?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Obviously, this is not your note, this is, we understand, and we'll hear from her tomorrow, [Dr B].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But you mentioned, I think, eight lines down -- if you want to refresh your memory from that section, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This is the note that you told us about before that [Dr B] made of what happened once you had gone back to [Baby P] and which you had refreshed your memory from.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I just wanted to give you the opportunity again. You've actually, I think, given us quite a detailed account of what happened, but just to check you've not missed anything.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. (Pause). It more or less covers what I've just said.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It more or less covers... There was a drop in sats, drop in heart rate. It also says, just a few minutes earlier, [Baby P] had been seen and the discussion was to do those bloods that I have just mentioned, so the gas, lactate, ammonia, CRP, and shortly after that [Baby P] deteriorated.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Does that suggest that after your examination of [Baby P] at 9.35, and we ran through your plan and I asked you to explain ammonia, that is something you then discussed with [Dr B]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think [Dr B] had already -- this is what you may have to find out from her directly. But yeah, I think we'd already discussed that, yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: It's just suggested by the note, but as I say, we'll hear from [Dr B].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: If we scroll down. [Baby P] deteriorated, Dr Ukoh started to bag, which is (overspeaking) Neopuff, as you've explained.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Which is what I explained, the Neopuff.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: "Intravenous access was lost as not flushing."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: "Airway maintained whilst intubation had been prepared."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then it goes on to describe the insertion of the intraosseous needle, first in left, then your name in brackets at the bottom, and then right and in brackets "Myself". So it's your recollection, is it, that thereafter you moved on to care for other babies in the unit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Right. Did you have cause to treat or see [Baby P] again during the course of that day?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I did not.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: I have no more questions if you could wait there, Dr .
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Dr Ukoh, I'd like to look at the note that you made at about 9.35, which is at tile 289. If we just scroll down to your entry, please. We'll go there, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: You explained to us the problems that you have listed at 1 to 5. At item 4 you have, "Apnoeas, bradys", and at number 5 you've got "Abd [or abdominal] distension". Do you know what period of [Baby P]'s life those apply to?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. Those applied within the -- because he was actually day 3 of life, so this was within the first -- so what I was referring to there was within the first 72 hours of his life.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Right. Do you recall whether they relate particularly to any problems that had happened during the course of the night shift, the shift that had started from 8 o'clock in the evening the day before through to this morning? Can you recall whether they applied to that or not?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I cannot fully recall, but because he wasn't on the CPAP anymore, I don't think it was something that occurred overnight because he would have been left on the CPAP machine.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: If we just have a look at the observation chart at tile 22 just with regard to what you say there. Just go into that. Pausing there, if we look overnight, can you see at the top, we're going to follow these columns down, where it says 23/6/16. The cursor is just there.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: You can see where it says 22, 22.00, just below and to the left of 23. Do you see the 22.00 where the cursor is?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Then we've got 22.00, then 00 which is midnight, 02, 04 and 06, through to 08 on the 24th, the handover on the 24th. Do you see that period there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: With that in mind I'm going to scroll down to the entries we have for how he was receiving air and down to the bottom part of the chart. If we look, just take a moment to look in on this, down the left-hand column in the handwritten entries you'll eventually see an entry saying "Optiflow"; can you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I can see that, yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: All right. Then if we go from left to right, go across to the Optiflow, there's nothing to start with, but we can see "Optiflow" above -- it's initialled "SE" down at the bottom, but can you see it says 4L or 4 litres?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I can see that, yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: That's there for five of those entries.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: If we just scroll up, if we put the cursor on the first one and scroll up, we can see what time they apply to.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can you see they run from 10 o'clock in the evening through to about 6 in the morning?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: So it's apparent he had to be put on breathing support round about 10 o'clock in the evening on the 23rd, didn't he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Although he was taken off it by 6 in the morning, we've seen that; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: So is it conceivable that would indicate some issue with regard to or some concern with regard to breathing overnight?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Possibly, but the fact that they were less concerned to take it off in the morning, in my opinion, would mean that they weren't particularly that concerned. I mean, every premature baby may have the odd desat or brady, but for them to have taken it off that morning would suggest they were less concerned with his respiratory status.
blocks.speaker: UKOH

blocks.text: Yes. Whoever had taken that decision, it would suggest that by 6 o'clock they were less concerned; is that fair to say?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I mean, it sounds like that I wasn't getting air and then I was getting air, but again it could be because of the tip of the NG tube had just moved or it could be also a new thing, it's hard to say.
blocks.speaker: ELLIS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Does your Lordship have any questions of Ms Ellis?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Just in relation to self-correcting bradycardias. How long do you leave it?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So sometimes, like I said, preterm babies do have bradycardias and desats, and that can be due to immaturity, it's not something to get complacent about, it's something to definitely keep an eye on. There probably isn't a time frame. I guess if it's going on for maybe 5, 10 seconds and they're not bringing themselves up then it may be you just give them a little bit of a nudge. If that doesn't bring them up then you'd need to increase your intervention, whether that be -- you know, if they are apnoeic, whether you start bagging them and giving them some breaths.
blocks.speaker: ELLIS

blocks.text: So it's 5 or 10 seconds and then if they've corrected themselves --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That's a very --
blocks.speaker: ELLIS

blocks.text: As a rough idea?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's hard to say. I think unless you're -- sometimes when you're in that situation you don't necessarily look at the time, you're just sort of thinking, "It's going on for a little bit now, maybe we should just give them a little bit of stimulation". But yeah, it's hard to say a definite time.
